theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of an agency's vision statement?
options: To list each unit's targets and budget lines for the coming year
To describe the future the agency is working towards
To set out the rules staff must follow in their daily work
To record the history of the agency since it was founded

questions.stem: A new chief executive officer (CEO) of a public agency wants staff in every parish office to understand its new vision. What should she do first?
options: Email the vision document to all managers and ask them to file it
Print the vision on posters and put them up in every office
Explain it in person, say why it matters and invite questions
Ask the human resource unit to add it to the staff handbook

questions.stem: Which statement best describes an organisation's mission, as opposed to its vision?
options: What it does, for whom and how, now
The future it hopes to reach in years to come
The amount it plans to spend in a year
The names of its board members and senior staff

questions.stem: A ministry has the values "integrity, service and respect" on its walls, but managers often ignore rude treatment of the public. What is the most likely effect?
options: Staff will follow the values more closely than before
The public will not notice how staff treat them at all
Managers will be seen as strong and decisive leaders
Staff will see the values as words that do not matter

questions.stem: Which action by a director most clearly shows the value of accountability in a public body?
options: Blaming a junior officer when a project goes wrong
Owning a mistake openly and explaining how it will be fixed
Keeping problems quiet until the end of the financial year
Asking the press office to issue a statement on her behalf

questions.stem: What is meant by an organisation's culture?
options: The shared beliefs, values and habits that shape how work is done
The art and music the organisation sponsors in the community
The written job descriptions held in the human resource unit
The number of staff from each parish who work for the body

questions.stem: Staff at a statutory body say, "Here, nobody takes a decision without the director's signature." The new director wants faster service. What should she do?
options: Sign more documents each day so the queue moves faster
Tell staff to stop asking for her signature on anything
Set clear limits for decisions at each level and back staff who use them
Hire more clerks to carry the papers to and from her office more quickly

questions.stem: Which sign suggests that a public agency has a healthy culture of learning?
options: Mistakes are hidden so that nobody is blamed
Only senior managers attend training each year
Projects are never reviewed once they are finished
Staff can raise problems and lessons are shared

questions.stem: A senior manager at a municipal corporation is on a tender panel. Her brother's company has bid. What should she do?
options: Declare the interest and step back from the panel
Stay on the panel but give her brother's bid an average score
Ask her brother to withdraw the bid quietly
Say nothing, since she will judge the bids fairly

questions.stem: A minister's adviser asks a director to speed up a permit for a political supporter, ahead of other applicants. What is the director's best response?
options: Agree, because the request has come straight from the minister's own office
Approve the permit but keep no record of the request at all
Politely explain that permits follow the set process, and record it
Pass the request to a junior officer to handle as they see fit

questions.stem: Why is political neutrality important for senior public servants?
options: It means public servants must never vote in national elections
It lets them serve any government fairly and keeps public trust
It allows them to ignore the policies of the government of the day
It means ministers cannot ask them for advice on any policy

questions.stem: A CEO asks all managers to cut travel costs by 20%, then books business-class flights for her own trip. What is the most likely effect on managers?
options: They will cut costs more than asked to make up for her
They will see that the rule applies equally to everyone
They will ask the board to raise the travel budget instead
They will doubt her commitment and take the cut less seriously

questions.stem: Which behaviour by senior leaders does most to build trust across a large public body?
options: Doing what they say they will do, and explaining decisions
Making all decisions behind closed doors to avoid argument
Speaking to staff only through written memos from head office
Visiting regional offices only when a problem has been reported

questions.stem: An agency's corporate plan aims to cut the time for business registration. Which unit plan best supports this?
options: The finance unit plans to repaint its offices this year
The registry unit plans to move all forms online by March
The transport unit plans to buy two new cars for officers
The training unit plans a course on office party planning

questions.stem: Why should a senior leader make sure each unit's work plan links to the corporate plan?
options: So that each unit can set its own direction freely
So that the corporate plan can be shorter each year
So all units pull the same way towards shared goals
So that unit managers no longer need to report results

questions.stem: A public body sets 24 targets in its corporate plan and meets 18 of them by year end. What percentage of targets did it meet?
The licensing and inspection units of an agency each blame the other for long delays. What is the best action for the director of operations?
options: Bring both teams together to map the process and fix it jointly
Ask each unit head to write a report on the other unit's failings
Merge the two units at once without talking to the staff
Leave each unit to solve its own part of the problem alone

questions.stem: What does "working in silos" mean in an organisation?
options: Units store their records in a central warehouse
Units work alone and share little with each other
Units take turns to lead the organisation each year
Units meet each week to plan work together

questions.stem: Which arrangement best helps several ministries deliver a joint programme on youth employment?
options: Each ministry runs its own version and reports separately
One ministry does all the work and the others watch
A joint steering group with shared goals and clear roles
The ministries meet once at the launch and not again

questions.stem: A director needs support from other directors, over whom she has no authority, for a new shared records system. What is the most effective approach?
options: Ask the CEO to order the other directors to agree
Go ahead in her own unit and wait for others to follow
Send a long technical paper to each of them and ask for a reply within a week
Learn each director's concerns and show how it helps their units

questions.stem: Why is building a network of relationships across the organisation useful to a senior leader?
options: It helps her gain support and information when it is needed
It means she no longer needs to follow agreed procedures
It replaces the need to report to the board or minister
It lets her avoid meetings with her own unit's staff

questions.stem: In a Jamaican ministry, which senior public servant is usually the administrative head and accounting officer?
options: The Minister
The Permanent Secretary
The Chief Personnel Officer of the unit
The Custos of the parish

questions.stem: A public agency plans to close two small rural offices. Which group should the leadership consult before deciding?
options: Only the agency's own finance staff
Only the people who work in the head office
Staff, unions, local users and community leaders
Only the media, so the news is out quickly and widely

questions.stem: What is a stakeholder map mainly used for?
options: Showing where each office of the body is located in the parish
Planning the routes that field officers will drive each week in the parish
Listing the assets and equipment owned by the organisation
Showing who is affected or has influence, and how to engage them

questions.stem: A CEO wants all 900 staff in 14 parish offices to hear about a major change on the same day. Which approach is best?
options: An all-staff video call, then managers brief teams the same day
A memo sent by post to each parish office over two weeks
Tell the head office staff and let the news spread from there
Post a short note on the intranet with no other message

questions.stem: Why should senior leaders create ways for staff to send ideas and concerns upward, not just receive messages?
options: So that front-line staff can make all the main decisions
So leaders learn what is really happening and staff feel heard
So that the board need not receive any further reports
So that managers have fewer meetings with their teams

questions.stem: Rumours of job cuts are spreading in an agency. The leadership has not made any decision. What should the CEO do?
options: Say nothing until a decision is made, to avoid more rumours
Deny the rumours firmly and promise that nobody will ever lose a job
Tell staff what is and is not known, and when they will hear more
Ask managers to find out who started the rumours

questions.stem: A senior leader wants managers across the organisation to take more initiative. Which step will help most?
options: Check every decision managers make before it is used
Ask managers to copy her on every email they send
Hold managers to account only when something goes wrong
Give clear goals and authority, then support their decisions

questions.stem: What is "distributed leadership" in an organisation?
options: Leadership shared among people at many levels, not just the top
A leader who travels between all the offices in turn
The handing out of leadership manuals to every staff member
A rule that each unit must elect its own manager each year

questions.stem: Junior officers at a ministry rarely point out errors in senior managers' plans. What should senior leaders do to change this?
options: Tell junior officers to speak up more in meetings
Welcome challenge, thank those who raise issues and act on them
Add a rule that all errors must be reported to the director in writing
Hold fewer meetings so that errors are not discussed

questions.stem: A leader who puts the needs of staff and the public first, and sees her role as helping others succeed, is showing which approach?
options: Autocratic leadership
Transactional leadership
Servant leadership
Laissez-faire leadership

questions.stem: Which statement best describes adaptive leadership?
options: Using the same approach in every situation without change
Following the rules exactly, whatever the circumstances
Leaving others to decide how to face every new challenge
Helping people face new challenges that have no ready answer

questions.stem: In Kotter's model for leading change, what is usually the first step?
options: Create a sense of urgency
Celebrate short-term wins
Anchor the change in the culture
Remove barriers to action

questions.stem: A public body is moving to digital records. Many long-serving staff are anxious. What should the leadership do to keep their support?
options: Bring in younger staff to replace those who are anxious
Involve them early, train them well and listen to concerns
Introduce the system quickly before anyone can object
Allow each office to decide whether to use the system

questions.stem: After a hurricane damages several parish offices, what should the agency's senior leadership do first?
options: Meet to write a new five-year corporate plan
Prepare the annual report to Parliament early
Check that all staff are safe and set up the emergency team
Ask each office to reopen at once whatever the damage to the building

questions.stem: During a crisis, why should leaders give staff and the public frequent, honest updates even when not everything is known?
options: So that the leaders do not have to make any decisions
So the media will stop asking questions of the body
So staff can be told to keep the information secret
So that trust is kept and rumours do not fill the gap

questions.stem: A senior leadership team must decide whether to move a service online. Which approach is best?
options: Gather evidence, consult users and staff, weigh risks, then decide
Decide quickly at one meeting based on what feels right to the CEO
Copy what another country did without checking if it fits
Wait for the minister to decide so the team is not blamed

questions.stem: After a major decision, why should senior leaders explain the reasons to staff, including those who disagree?
options: So that staff can vote again on the decision
So staff understand it, even if they would have chosen differently
So that nobody in the organisation can ever question the decision again
So that the leaders can avoid putting it in writing

questions.stem: A balanced scorecard helps leaders track an organisation's performance by looking at which kinds of measures?
options: Financial measures only, such as spending against the approved budget
Staff attendance only, across all of the units
Financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth
The number of meetings held by each unit in a month

questions.stem: In a staff engagement survey, 420 of an agency's 600 staff responded. What was the response rate?
A public body expects several directors to retire within three years. What should the senior leadership do now?
options: Identify and develop managers who could take on those roles
Wait until the directors leave and then advertise the posts
Ask the retiring directors to stay on for as long as they can
Plan to merge the directors' units when they leave

questions.stem: Which programme is most likely to build strong leaders across a ministry?
options: A single lecture on leadership theory for new managers
Coaching, stretch assignments, learning sets and feedback
A reading list sent by email to all senior managers
A yearly award for the manager with the lowest costs

questions.stem: What is the main role of the board of a statutory body in relation to its CEO?
options: To run the day-to-day operations of the body instead of the CEO
To approve every purchase the CEO's staff make
To set direction, hold the CEO to account and oversee risk
To act only as an advisory group with no real duties

questions.stem: An internal audit finds weak controls over overtime payments across several units. What should the CEO do?
options: Ask the auditors to soften the wording of the report
Wait to see whether next year's audit finds the same problem again
Tell each unit to sort it out in its own way
Accept the findings, agree actions and track them to completion

questions.stem: How can a senior leadership team best judge how well it is leading the organisation?
options: Use results, staff surveys and stakeholder feedback, and act on them
Count how many speeches and office visits the leaders made in the year
Rely on what the leaders believe about their own work
Look only at whether the year's budget was spent in full

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What two-word term names a short statement of the future an organisation is working towards?
What two-word term names a statement of what an organisation does, for whom and how?
What two-word term describes the shared beliefs, values and habits that shape how work is done in an organisation?
What one word describes units that work in isolation and share little with the rest of the organisation?
What two-word term describes leadership that puts serving staff and the public first?
What two-word term describes leadership shared across many people and levels of an organisation?
What two-word name is given to the tool that tracks performance under financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth headings?
Whose eight-step model for leading change begins with creating a sense of urgency?
What two-word term describes a workplace where staff feel safe to speak up, ask questions and admit mistakes?
In a Jamaican ministry, what is the title of the senior public servant who is the administrative head?
What word describes any person or group who is affected by, or can influence, an organisation's work?
An agency met 27 of its 36 corporate targets. What percentage of targets did it meet?
In a staff survey, 360 of 450 staff replied. What was the response rate, as a percentage?
What two-word term names an open meeting where senior leaders brief all staff and take their questions?
What three-word term describes a situation where a leader's personal interests could affect their official decisions?

essays.stem: A newly merged public agency has staff from two former bodies with different ways of working. As its CEO, plan how you would develop and embed a shared vision and values in the first year.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by listening. In the first month I would visit offices from both former bodies, hold small group meetings and run a short survey to learn what staff value, what worries them and what each body did well. I would also seek the views of the board, the ministry and key users of our services. I would then form a working group drawn from both bodies and all levels to draft a vision of the future we want and three to five values, each described as behaviours, such as "we answer every customer within two days". The draft would go out for comment before the board approves it. To embed it, I would launch the vision in person at town hall meetings in each region, and ask every manager to discuss with their team what it means for their work. The values would be built into recruitment, induction, appraisal and recognition. Most important, I and the senior team would model the values daily and act when they are broken. At the end of the year I would check progress through a staff survey and service results.
markingPoints: Listens to staff from both bodies and to stakeholders first
Uses a mixed working group to draft the vision and behaviour-based values, with consultation
Launches the vision visibly and has managers translate it for their teams
Builds the values into HR systems such as recruitment, appraisal and recognition
Models the values personally and reviews progress with evidence

essays.stem: Staff surveys at a statutory body show a culture of blame: people hide mistakes and avoid decisions. Evaluate the effects of this culture and recommend how senior leaders could change it.
essays.modelAnswer: A culture of blame harms the organisation in many ways. Because mistakes are hidden, small problems grow into large ones and the same errors are repeated. Staff avoid taking decisions, so every matter is passed upward, service slows and senior leaders are overloaded. New ideas are not raised because people fear failure. Morale falls, good staff leave, and the public receives poorer service. Changing this culture must start at the top. Senior leaders should openly admit their own mistakes and explain what they learned. They should respond to problems by asking "what happened and how do we fix it?" rather than "who is to blame?", while still dealing firmly with misconduct or repeated carelessness. Clear limits on who can decide what would give managers confidence to act. Reviews after projects and incidents should focus on learning, and lessons should be shared widely. Leaders should thank staff who raise problems early and recognise sensible risk-taking. Managers would need training to lead in this way. Progress should be tracked through staff surveys, the number of issues reported and decision times.
markingPoints: Explains effects: hidden and repeated errors
Explains effects: slow decisions, overloaded leaders, fewer ideas, low morale
Recommends leaders model openness and a learning response, while handling misconduct
Recommends clear decision limits, learning reviews and recognition of those who raise problems
Includes manager training and measures to track the change

essays.stem: Explain why ethical leadership matters in the public service, and describe how a senior leader can promote integrity across a ministry.
essays.modelAnswer: Public servants spend public money and make decisions that affect people's lives, so the public must be able to trust them. Ethical leadership protects that trust. When leaders act with honesty, fairness and openness, staff are more likely to do the same, resources are used for their proper purpose, and decisions are made on merit rather than favour. When leaders behave unethically, corruption and waste spread, good staff become cynical, and the ministry's reputation suffers. A senior leader can promote integrity in several ways. First, by setting an example: declaring her own interests, refusing improper gifts and following procedures even under pressure. Second, by making the rules clear: a code of conduct, a gifts and conflicts register, and procurement and recruitment rules that everyone understands. Third, through training using real dilemmas staff may face. Fourth, by giving staff a safe way to report concerns, protecting those who report in good faith, and acting on reports. Fifth, by supporting internal audit and acting on its findings. Finally, she should recognise staff who do the right thing, even when it is difficult.
markingPoints: Explains that ethical leadership protects public trust and proper use of resources
Explains the harm of unethical leadership (corruption, cynicism, reputation)
Describes leading by example, including declaring interests
Describes clear rules, registers and training on real dilemmas
Describes safe reporting, protection of reporters, audit and recognition

essays.stem: Different units of a large agency work in silos, causing delays and duplicated work for the public. Recommend how senior leaders should improve collaboration across the organisation.
essays.modelAnswer: First, senior leaders must show that collaboration matters by working as one team themselves, sharing information and solving problems together at leadership meetings rather than defending their own units. They should set some shared goals, for example the total time a customer waits from first contact to final approval, so that units are judged on the whole result, not just their own part. Next, they could bring staff from the units together to map the main processes from the customer's point of view and remove duplicated steps and hand-off delays. Cross-unit project teams could tackle specific problems, with a sponsor from senior management. Shared systems, such as one case management system, would let each unit see the status of a file. Regular joint meetings between managers of linked units would help them plan together. Staff could be offered short placements in other units to understand their work. Appraisals for managers should include how well they work with other units, and leaders should recognise good examples of collaboration. Progress should be measured through customer waiting times and staff feedback.
markingPoints: Senior team models collaboration itself
Sets shared goals and measures across units
Maps processes jointly and uses cross-unit teams
Uses shared systems, joint meetings or staff placements
Builds collaboration into appraisal and recognition, and measures progress

essays.stem: A cyber attack shuts down a public agency's computer systems for several days, stopping services to the public. Describe how the senior leadership should lead the organisation through the crisis.
essays.modelAnswer: The first step is to activate the agency's emergency or business continuity plan and form a small crisis team with clear roles: a leader, IT and security, communications, operations and legal advice. The team should meet often and keep a log of decisions. It should work with IT specialists to contain the attack, protect data and restore systems safely, and report the incident to the proper authorities. Because personal data may be at risk, the data protection law and any duty to notify must be followed. Meanwhile, leaders should find ways to keep the most important services running, for example with paper forms, manual records and priority appointments. Communication is vital. Staff should get regular, honest updates on what is known, what to do and what not to do, such as not using affected devices. The public, the ministry and the media should be told clearly what has happened, which services are affected and when they will hear more, without guessing. Leaders should be visible and support stressed staff. Afterwards, the agency should review what happened, fix weaknesses and share the lessons.
markingPoints: Activates the continuity plan and sets up a crisis team with roles and a decision log
Contains the attack, protects data and follows reporting and data protection duties
Keeps essential services running by other means
Gives regular, honest updates to staff, the public, the ministry and the media
Supports staff and holds a lessons-learned review afterwards

essays.stem: As a director with no authority over other directors, you want them to adopt a shared customer service standard across the organisation. Describe how you would gain their support.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by preparing a strong case, using facts such as complaint figures, waiting times and customer survey results that show the problem and the benefit to each unit. Before any formal meeting, I would meet each director one-to-one to listen to their concerns and priorities, because people support ideas they have helped to shape. I would show how the standard helps their own goals, for example by reducing complaints that take up their managers' time. I would invite one or two respected directors to work with me on the draft, so it becomes a shared proposal rather than mine alone. Where there are concerns, such as extra workload, I would look for compromises, perhaps a phased start or a pilot in willing units. I would then present the joint proposal at the leadership meeting, with the CEO's support but not relying on an order from the top. Once agreed, I would help others put it in place, share early results and give credit to the units that improve. Throughout, I would keep my promises and stay open, which builds trust for future work.
markingPoints: Builds a case using evidence of the problem and benefits
Meets directors individually to understand concerns and priorities
Shows how it serves their goals and co-designs with respected peers
Offers compromises such as a pilot or phased start
Gains formal agreement, supports roll-out, shares credit and builds trust

essays.stem: Plan a leadership development programme for middle managers across a government ministry, and explain how you would judge whether it has worked.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first agree with the senior team what kind of leaders the ministry needs, linked to its plan and values, for example managers who lead change, work across units and develop their staff. I would then assess the current managers against this, using appraisals, 360-degree feedback and self-assessment, to find the main gaps. The programme would run over about a year and mix methods, because leaders learn most by doing. It would include short workshops on topics such as leading change, ethical decisions and coaching staff; a stretch assignment for each manager, such as leading a cross-unit project; a coach or mentor from senior management; and small learning groups that meet monthly to discuss real problems. Each manager would have a personal development plan agreed with their own manager, who would support them. Senior leaders would open sessions to show the programme matters. To judge whether it worked, I would look at participants' feedback, changes in their 360-degree scores, results of their projects, staff survey results in their teams, and how many go on to more senior roles.
markingPoints: Defines the leadership needed, linked to the ministry's plan and values
Assesses current managers to find the gaps
Uses a mix of methods: workshops, stretch assignments, coaching and learning groups
Uses personal development plans with line manager and senior leader support
Evaluates with feedback, behaviour change, results and progression

essays.stem: Compare transformational and transactional leadership, and recommend which approach a senior leader in a public body should use.
essays.modelAnswer: Transactional leadership is based on clear exchanges: the leader sets tasks, targets and rules, and staff are rewarded for meeting them or corrected when they do not. It gives order, clear expectations and control, which matter in a public body where procedures, financial rules and accountability are important. Its weakness is that it may get compliance rather than commitment, and staff may do only what is measured. Transformational leadership inspires staff with a shared vision, sets an example, encourages new ideas and develops people. It can raise motivation, creativity and loyalty, and it helps an organisation through major change. Its weakness is that it depends on the leader's personal qualities, and without clear systems, enthusiasm may not turn into consistent results. In my view a senior public leader should use both. Transformational leadership is needed to give purpose, build a culture of service and lead change, such as moving services online. Transactional elements are needed to make sure rules are followed, money is controlled and targets are met. The best leaders inspire people and also keep clear systems of accountability.
markingPoints: Describes transactional leadership with a strength
Notes the weakness of transactional leadership (compliance, not commitment)
Describes transformational leadership with a strength
Notes the weakness of transformational leadership (depends on the person, needs systems)
Recommends combining both in a public body, with reasons

essays.stem: A public agency's leadership must win support for a plan to merge several small parish offices into larger service centres. Describe how they should engage stakeholders across and outside the organisation.
essays.modelAnswer: The leadership should begin by mapping stakeholders: staff and their unions, managers of the affected offices, the board and the ministry, local users of the services, community leaders, councillors and members of parliament for the areas, and partner agencies. For each, they should consider how much they are affected and how much influence they have, and plan how to engage them. Staff should hear first, in person, from senior leaders, with clear reasons, what will happen to jobs and a chance to ask questions; unions should be consulted early as required. The board and ministry need a strong business case. Local users and community leaders should be consulted through meetings in each affected area, at times people can attend, and through a simple survey. Their concerns, such as travel costs for elderly users, should be taken seriously, and the plan changed where possible, for example with mobile services or online options. Leaders should explain how views shaped the final plan and keep everyone informed throughout. Throughout, they should be honest about what is fixed and what is still open to change.
markingPoints: Maps stakeholders inside and outside the organisation by impact and influence
Informs staff first in person and consults unions early
Provides a business case for the board and ministry
Consults users and community leaders accessibly and adjusts the plan
Reports back how views shaped the plan and stays honest and informative

essays.stem: Evaluate the ways a senior leadership team can gather evidence on how well it is leading a public organisation, and recommend a review approach.
essays.modelAnswer: A leadership team can use several kinds of evidence, each with strengths and limits. Organisational results, such as corporate plan targets and service times, show whether the organisation is achieving its purpose, but they can be affected by factors outside leaders' control. Staff engagement surveys show how staff feel about direction, communication and trust; they are useful for trends but depend on a good response rate and honest answers, so they must be anonymous. 360-degree feedback on individual leaders gives a rounded view of their behaviour but must be handled with care. Feedback from stakeholders, such as the ministry, board, partners and the public, shows how the organisation is seen from outside. Audit reports and complaint trends show whether controls and service are working. Staff turnover and exit interviews can reveal problems with leadership. I would recommend a yearly review that brings these sources together on a single page, compares them with the previous year, and is discussed openly by the leadership team and board. The team should agree a few actions, share them with staff, and check progress during the year.
markingPoints: Evaluates organisational results as evidence, with a limit
Evaluates staff surveys and 360-degree feedback, with care needed
Evaluates stakeholder feedback, audits, complaints or turnover data
Recommends bringing sources together in a regular review
Recommends agreed actions, sharing with staff and follow-up

practical1.title: Develop a vision, values and leadership charter for a public agency
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case about a made-up Jamaican public agency (for example a newly merged agency that registers and supports small businesses, with offices in five parishes). Its staff survey shows low trust, poor communication between units and slow decisions. Acting as the senior leadership team, prepare a leadership pack for the agency. Give each member a named role: CEO (chairs the group, writes the vision statement and opens the presentation), values lead (writes three to five values, each with two behaviours that staff and leaders will show), communication lead (writes a plan to launch the vision across all offices: who, what, when and how, including upward channels for staff views), culture and collaboration lead (writes three practical actions to break down silos and speed up decisions, with owners and dates), and measures lead (chooses four to six measures to check progress, with a baseline from the case and a target). In a group of four, the CEO also writes the measures. Put the pack on flipchart sheets or slides and present it to the assessor, who plays the board, in 15 minutes. Every member presents their part and answers questions.
materials: Case pack from the assessor, including the staff survey results
Computers with presentation and word processor software, or flipchart paper and markers
photos: The values, each with its behaviours
The collaboration actions with owners and dates
The measures with baselines and targets
The group presenting to the board
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the pack
Vision is clear, inspiring and fits the agency's purpose
Values are described as observable behaviours
Communication plan reaches all offices and includes ways for staff to respond
Collaboration actions are practical, with owners and dates
Measures have sensible baselines from the case and realistic targets
Presented clearly and answered the board's questions
safety: Use only the made-up case; do not name real agencies, officials or staff
Keep the case survey data confidential to the group and assessor
Respect each other's views; challenge ideas, not people
Share the workload fairly and take a short break

practical2.title: Lead a cross-department crisis response meeting and brief all staff
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a crisis case for a made-up public body (for example a hurricane has damaged two parish offices of a government agency, the records system is down and staff in one area cannot be reached). Your group is the senior leadership team. Give each member a named role: chair (leads the crisis meeting and keeps it to the agenda and time), operations director (reports on offices and services and proposes how to keep key services running), people director (reports on staff safety and welfare and proposes support), communications director (drafts the all-staff message and a short public notice), and recorder (keeps the decision and action log and checks that every action has an owner and a time). In a group of four, the chair also keeps the log. Hold a 30-minute crisis meeting. Partway through, the assessor will give an update card that changes the situation, and the team must adjust its plan. After the meeting, finalise the all-staff message and the public notice, and the chair gives a 3-minute spoken briefing to the assessor as if to all staff.
materials: Crisis case and update card from the assessor
Agenda and decision and action log templates
Computer with word processor software and printer
Table and chairs set up as a meeting room
photos: The agenda and each director's prepared notes

checklist: Took a named role and prepared for it from the case
Put staff safety first and agreed how to reach missing staff
Agreed practical ways to keep key services running
Responded sensibly to the update card and changed the plan
Every decision in the log has an owner and a time
Messages are honest, clear and say when the next update will come
safety: Use only the made-up case; do not refer to real disasters, victims or officials
Keep the case and notes confidential to the group and assessor
The case may remind some people of real events: anyone may step out, and the assessor will check in
Photograph faces only if every person agrees and the Centre allows it
Take a short break after the meeting
